questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a dictionary still need standards even though INFORMATION_SCHEMA auto-generates much of it?
options: Because the values those fields contain (like column names) can still vary wildly across tables built by different teams
Because INFORMATION_SCHEMA is unreliable and often returns incorrect data
Because standards are only needed for manually-entered fields, never automated ones
Because SQL Server requires a separate license for standardized dictionaries
questions.explain: The schema is auto-documented, but one table might use CustID and another customer_id for the same concept — consistency still has to be deliberately maintained.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three dictionary standards this lesson names?
options: Mandatory description coverage for every table and column
Requiring every table to have exactly ten columns
Banning the use of INFORMATION_SCHEMA entirely
Requiring all tables to use the same primary key value
questions.explain: The three standards are naming convention compliance, mandatory description coverage, and terminology consistency with the glossary — a dictionary that's only 40% documented is not 40% useful.

questions.q: What does 'terminology consistency' mean in this lesson's context?
options: Dictionary descriptions should use the glossary's exact wording when referencing a business concept, not independently reinvent the phrasing
Every column name must be written in all capital letters
Descriptions must be written in a language other than English
Only one person in the entire organization is allowed to write descriptions
questions.explain: If the glossary defines 'Active Customer' a certain way, dictionary descriptions referencing that concept should use the same term, enforcing the glossary-dictionary link from Lesson 11.

questions.q: In the worked before/after example, what changed about the IsActiveFlag column's description, beyond just adding text?
options: The column was renamed to follow the naming standard, hedging language was removed, and it was explicitly linked to the glossary term it implements
The column's data type was changed from BIT to VARCHAR
The column was deleted entirely
Nothing changed except the font used to display it
questions.explain: cust_active became IsActiveFlag (naming fixed), vague hedging was removed, and the description explicitly referenced the Active Customer glossary definition.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is 'a dictionary standard' a brand-new concept introduced for the first time in this course?
options: No — it's the application of Data Governance Foundations' naming standards and this course's own metadata standards, specifically to the dictionary artifact
Yes — it has no connection to anything covered earlier in the Data Governance path
No — it only applies to Oracle databases, never SQL Server
Yes — it replaces the need for a business glossary entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects dictionary standards back to Data Governance Foundations' naming conventions and this course's metadata standards from Lesson 3.
